lesson.title: False Alarms: The Biology of Panic Disorder
lesson.summary: Panic disorder involves recurrent, unexpected panic attacks along with persistent worry about future attacks, and it can be understood as the body's fight-flight-freeze response firing when there is no actual danger present.
lesson.body:
A panic attack is an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort that peaks within minutes, accompanied by at least four of a specific set of physical and cognitive symptoms: a pounding heart, sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, a choking sensation, chest pain, nausea, dizziness or lightheadedness, chills or heat sensations, tingling or numbness, feelings of unreality or detachment from oneself, fear of losing control or going crazy, and fear of dying. Panic disorder is diagnosed when a person has recurrent, unexpected panic attacks, meaning attacks that are not reliably triggered by a specific external cue, and at least one attack is followed by a month or more of persistent worry about having additional attacks or about their consequences, or by a significant change in behavior aimed at avoiding them.

The clearest way to understand what is happening physiologically during a panic attack is through the fight-flight-freeze response. That response evolved to prepare the body to react quickly to real danger: the heart speeds up to move blood to the muscles, breathing quickens to increase oxygen, and attention narrows sharply onto the perceived threat. A panic attack involves essentially the same system activating in full, with the same racing heart, rapid breathing, and surge of fear, except that there is no external danger triggering it. This is part of why panic attacks are often described as false alarms, and also why they can be so disorienting: the body is behaving exactly as if it were in mortal danger while the mind cannot identify any actual threat to explain it.

This is also what distinguishes panic disorder from a specific phobia. A phobia's fear is reliably cued by a particular object or situation, so the person generally knows what will trigger it and can predict when they are at risk. Panic disorder, by contrast, is defined by attacks that seem to come out of nowhere, which is what fuels the second half of the diagnosis: persistent anxiety about when the next one will strike, since there is no obvious cue to avoid. A well documented clinical pattern illustrates how disorienting this can be: people experiencing their first panic attack frequently go to an emergency room convinced they are having a heart attack, given how closely the physical symptoms can resemble one, only to have cardiac tests come back entirely normal. That gap, between how dangerous the attack feels and how safe the body actually is, is precisely the false alarm at the center of panic disorder.
